scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

The situation involves a custody arrangement where the father has every other weekend and a weekday. The ex is using the "for the son's sake" excuse to adjust the schedule, and the father has been accommodating. Now, the father is asserting his rights by not giving up his scheduled time for the ex's family events.

First, I need to consider the legal aspect. The custody arrangement was decided by court, so both parents have to follow the schedule unless there's a modification. The father has been allowing changes, but now he's pushing back. The ex is taking the kids to a lake and an amusement park, which might be outside the agreed-upon schedule. The father wants to ensure he gets his scheduled time, which he's been giving up before. 

Morally, the father is trying to protect his own time with his son, which is part of the custody agreement. The ex is using the child's interests to justify changing the schedule, which could be manipulative. The father's action of asserting his rights might be seen as standing up for himself and ensuring the child's time with him isn't compromised. However, the ex might feel that the father is being selfish by not giving up his time for family events. 

But the key here is that the custody arrangement is legal, and the father has a right to his scheduled time. The ex's actions might be violating the court order by not following the agreed schedule. The father's refusal to give up his time could be a necessary step to enforce the legal agreement. So morally, it's acceptable because he's upholding the agreed-upon terms, even if it's uncomfortable. The ex's behavior might be the issue, not the father's decision to protect his time. 

However, there's a possibility that the father's actions could be seen as being inconsiderate if he's not making exceptions for the child's needs. But since the child is already getting time with the mother, the father's time is also important. The ex's insistence on changing the schedule might be more about control than the child's well-being. Therefore, the father's decision to keep his son during his scheduled time is morally acceptable.
